Row Together
5 AM. Your kit bag is packed. Your other bag is also packed. You're standing between them like a man between two trains.
I heard. I'm sorry. The decider is in two days. Lose it and we're out of the World Cup.
I won't tell you to stay. I flew home in 2019 when my father was ill. I'd do it again. Whatever you choose, nobody in this team will say a word.
Stay and play.
Amma asked you to.
Call Shibu first.
He'll tell you the truth.
Don't come. I'm serious. What will you do here, lift wood? We have a hundred people lifting wood. We have ONE person playing in the World Cup.
Your father's rule. Row together. You row there. We row here.
Video call, the next morning. The storm has gone. The sky is washed clean. And on the jetty there are a hundred and twelve people.

Fishermen. The church choir. Three boat-race crews. The tea-shop grandmother. Children carrying coconut rope. Father Joseph in rubber boots. They are pulling the Lakshmi upright with ropes, in rhythm, singing the old rowing song.
Look at them. I fed every one of these people. Twenty years. I never asked anyone for anything.
I didn't have to ask.
Your match fee arrived.
Amma tried to send it back.
I hid her phone.
The decider. Win and you're in the quarter-final. Lose and everyone goes home. You come in at three down, and stay there for thirty-five overs.
Before the last over, you look at the camera, touch your collar, and then mime pulling an oar. Twice. In Kuttanad, a hundred and twelve people with rope burns on their hands start to cry.
10 off 6
Win or go home. A hundred and twelve people just lifted your mother's boat out of a river. Ten to win.
INTO THE QUARTERS!
Kuttanad rings every church and temple bell at once.
OUT!
Harpreet, the last man, swings the final ball for four.
Six, then four. Done with a ball to spare. Sameer runs onto the field before the umpire has even moved. He picks you up. Physically. Off the ground.
QUARTER-FINAL!

Caught on the rope, three short. You walk off sure that you've just ended the World Cup for everyone. Then Harpreet, who has scored eleven runs in two years, closes his eyes and swings. Four. Through. By one run.
You built that! Every run of it! Harpreet just hit the last nail. Don't you dare look sad!
Back in the hotel, there's a note under your door. Not hotel paper this time. A business card. On the back, in very neat writing: "Breakfast? We need to talk about your future. F.K."
Quarter-final in three days. And Faisal Kutty has decided to play his last card.
